title: Surrogate who refused abortion over heart defect takes custody battle to US Supreme Court
description: A surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in the dispu
body: A surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute over who should have custody of the baby. McKenna West filed an emergency appeal asking the court to halt a previous ruling granting parental rights to California couple Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.Ahmed and Gilkar had asked West to abort the pregnancy after a scan at 20 weeks showed the foetus had a severe heart defect. Instead, West - who has been supported by several Republican officials - travelled to Texas where nearly all abortions are illegal and gave birth to the child. The BBC has contacted lawyers for Ahmed and Gilkar for comment. West has since been pushing for custody over the baby, born last month with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a defect where the left side of the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body. The condition often requires multiple surgeries, which are not a cure. Infants with the condition can have lifelong complications, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. After West travelled to the state, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and won an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive medical care in the state. He had surgery soon after birth. West said she denied the couple's requests to have the abortion after learning of treatment options and wanting to keep "this precious baby", according to the Supreme Court filing. West has argued that the biological parents should not have custody because she worries they would not give the boy necessary medical care because they sought to abort the child after learning of the life-threatening condition. In a previous court hearing, Gilkar said the baby - whom they named Rumi - was "our child" and "the love of our lives", according to the Associated Press. They said West travelled to Texas without telling them and blocked their access to medical information. A California court previously granted parental rights to Ahmed and Gilkar, while a Texas court issued a restraining order blocking West from seeing the baby. Last month, an attorney for the California couple said the child was in critical condition and seemed to be "suffering from potential complications".West argued that without intervention from the Supreme Court, she would no longer have access to information about the child's medical condition.  In the filing, lawyers for West suggested that the California couple could place the child in hospice care.

schema.headline: Surrogate who refused abortion over heart defect takes custody battle to US Supreme Court

title: England vs Pakistan: Alastair Cook and Michael Vaughan question Joe Root tactics in Razaullah onslaught
description: England had "no plan" and were "out of control" in the face of Razaullah's stunning hitting on the third day of the final Test against Pakistan, accor
body: England had "no plan" and were "out of control" in the face of Razaullah's stunning hitting on the third day of the final Test against Pakistan, according to former captain Alastair Cook.Razaullah, the 21-year-old batting at number nine on Test debut, clobbered 81 from 63 balls at Edgbaston.He shared a ninth-wicket partnership of 121 with Muhammad Abbas to drag the third Test into an unlikely fourth day, with England set 130 for victory.Though the hosts are heavy favourites to earn a 3-0 clean sweep, the carnage of the final session was an alarming spell as Joe Root begins his second spell as captain.Root's tactics were often criticised in his first spell as skipper and there were further questions of the Yorkshireman when he stood in for former captain Ben Stokes earlier this summer."You can get done by the tail - it's very hard when people have the license and ability to hit sixes," Cook told Test Match Special. "What I saw was no plan, it got out of control."That's when you need the backroom staff and coaches to step up. I would loved to have seen a message and some real leadership from the coaches."England are currently led by interim head coach Marcus Trescothick, with New Zealander Stephen Fleming due to take on the role from December's tour of South Africa.Trescothick is assisted by bowling coach Tim Southee, who was seen on the boundary rope at times during the partnership. England's tactics were curious throughout the Razaullah-Abbas partnership. The seamers often stuck to a short-ball plan, with fielders back on the boundary. When their pace bowlers tried to hit the stumps, they could not find the target.More bizarre was Root giving the second new-ball to part-time off-spinner Dan Lawrence, who had barely bowled in the series to that point. In doing so, Root bowled Lawrence in front of seamer Ollie Robinson, who has had a sensational summer as England's attack leader.Jonathan Agnew, the former England fast bowler and the BBC's chief cricket commentator, called the tactics "appalling"."You cannot and should not bowl like that to tailenders as soon as they come in," he said."You have to set the tone when you're bowling against tailenders. Yes, you bowl aggressively, but in a controlled way. They are numbers nine and 10 for a reason. It was bitterly disappointing."Dan Lawrence is a part-time off-spinner and he took the second new-ball. If you're looking for any aspect of the day that is utterly bonkers, that is it."Razaullah's thrilling knock included nine sixes, tying the record for the most maximums in an innings by a batter on Test debut.He also equalled Stokes' record for the most sixes in a Test played in England.There were times when Root looked devoid of ideas, while the energy was sapped from his team. Jofra Archer cut a frustrated figure when Razaullah hit him for successive straight sixes and at one point Gus Atkinson was asked to bowl bouncers with eight fielders on the boundary."We shouldn't be surprised by England, they've delivered tactically like this on a regular basis," said ex-England captain Michael Vaughan."I think they'll win this game but they can't keep making mistakes like that. The basics of Test cricket generally work and that's to hit the top of the stumps. It's a bit of a warning sign that this attack is very good but they aren't the finished article just yet."Who are the characters in the team who are going got grab a hold of everyone and say, 'right, I'm going to make a moment'. I didn't see it from anyone today."At one stage Root left the field for an opportunity to consult with the England backroom staff, although it did little to alter the course of the evening.Eventually, Abbas poked the pace of Josh Tongue to point before Razaullah was stumped off Lawrence from the final ball of the day to leave Pakistan 453 all out."I'm disappointed, of course," said Trescothick. "We were in a position where they were eight down and the scores were level. We were hoping to go through them pretty quickly."We tried many different things. You have variations of plans. We bowled the short ball for a period of time, then length for a period of time, then a bit of spin. You're always chopping and changing, with various ideas."You'd always like to think you can do it better and you analyse it afterwards saying, 'right, was there an area or tactic we missed to get it right?' You hope in those situations when you bowl it in the right place, which we did on many occasions, that you get the nick or bowl them. Fair play, they played pretty well."

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: Alastair Cook and Michael Vaughan question Joe Root tactics in Razaullah onslaught

title: Sweden election becomes tight race, as hard right eyes role in government
description: Sweden's left- and right wing political blocs are in a tight race in Sunday's general election, with current conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristerss
body: Sweden's left- and right wing political blocs are in a tight race in Sunday's general election, with current conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson promising cabinet jobs for hard-right allies if he remains at the helm.Latest polls show a narrow lead for the left grouping, which is backing the Social Democrats' Magdalena Andersson to return to power.Kristersson has been supported in government by the hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), who have neo-Nazi roots.National security, gang crime and welfare spending are among the key issues, but the potential for the anti-immigration SD to enter government could also influence the outcome.In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.More than eight million people are eligible to vote in the election for Sweden's Riksdag. A poll on Friday, commissioned by Swedish news service Ekot, shows the left-wing bloc with 50.8% of the vote, compared with the right-wing bloc on 47.6% - a lead of 3.2%.The centre-left Social Democrats, who have pledged higher public spending, lead the polls, with 28.6%, while on the right the Sweden Democrats are behind them with 18.3%, according to the Ekot survey.Other opinion polls on Friday also put the left-wing bloc in the lead.The Social Democrats have regularly led Swedish governments since World War Two and have been the country's dominant political force for much of the last century.In stark comparison the SD, founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s, were for decades shunned by the mainstream.But the last election in 2022 marked a watershed moment, with the SD becoming Sweden's second largest party following a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.They have since offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which has overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy, including the abolition of permanent residency for refugees and increased deportations. But the party's MPs have never held ministerial roles.The Sweden Democrats have experienced controversies during this election campaign, including allegations that a party official spread pro-Russian messages on social media.Kristersson has said the official should be fired if the claims turn out to be true, while SD leader Jimmie Åkesson said the party was investigating the allegations.Nicholas Aylott, associate professor of political science at Södertörn University, told the BBC that the party getting into government "would be another big step in the normalisation of the party", but added that it was not the main issue for voters."That said, it might still be important for the election outcome," he said.Aylott explained that some voters who would have backed centre-right parties may well switch allegiance to the opposition, because they are put off by the prospect of SD ministers.Although he thought they would be few in number, "they might just tip the balance against the incumbent right-wing bloc", he said.This weekend's election comes a week after Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came close to winning a majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.They topped the poll with almost 44% of the vote, and their local leader Ulrich Siegmund says he is in talks with another party and other MPs in the hope of taking control of parliament.

schema.headline: Sweden election becomes tight race, as hard right eyes role in government

title: Donald Trump: Protests expected as US President visits Ireland
description: An avid golf fan, in July Trump said he hoped to travel to Doonbeg to watch the Irish Open.In a special video message, he told the US Embassy's Fourth
body: An avid golf fan, in July Trump said he hoped to travel to Doonbeg to watch the Irish Open.In a special video message, he told the US Embassy's Fourth of July celebration event that he wants to see "Rory [McIlroy] and all the great players"."There's nothing better than Irish-American friendship and I have a beautiful place over there - it's one of the best, most beautiful golf courses anywhere in the world," said Trump in his message, which was broadcast on a large screen."We have a place that's so top and we have the Irish Open going to be there. "They call it Trump National, we sometimes use the name of the location, but it's Trump National Golf Club, and we're looking forward to it."We're going to have a tremendous celebration. I think I'm going to come over and I'm going to see it and watch. It'll be something very, very special."President Connolly, an outspoken Gaza activist who has been critical of the US and said Trump is acting "like a bully" over tariffs, has come under pressure to raise issues in the Middle East during her brief meeting with the US president.Sinn Féin and a series of other parties in the Republic who backed her in the Irish presidency campaign last year have called on her to raise Gaza during her meeting with Trump.Ireland is one of the most pro-Palestinian countries in the European Union and has been criticised for its stance by Israel.

schema.headline: Donald Trump: Protests expected as US President visits Ireland

title: I couldn't experience my baby scan but blind parents like me can now feel them
description: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the h
body: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".But he said the 20-week scan was more positive."The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs."I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says."It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real."It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting.Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler.I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario.But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face.For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children.For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book.Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control."I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says.For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described.Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch.But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle.Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability"."We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says.Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives.They include things like:Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at handWhen changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feelScore a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them toUse a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get aroundOnce they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at homeWhen weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floorThe Royal National Institute of Blind People , external(RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children.They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door.For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot."I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision."One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside."When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off".For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible.Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them.

schema.headline: I couldn't experience my baby scan but blind parents like me can now feel them

title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
description: "Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told th
body: "Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria."So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal)."Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally.""This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats."They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday."But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025."They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.But would the US want to get involved anyway?President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 -  can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei."Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

schema.headline: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war

title: Children and a woman injured on Maltby fairground ride
description: Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said. Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags
body: Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said. Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening, which closed early after the incident.South Yorkshire Police said three people, aged 11, 13 and 21, had been taken to hospital for treatment. The extent of their injuries is not yet clear.Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground, the force added, with the road since reopening.Yorkshire Ambulance Service confirmed the two injured children were taken to Sheffield Children's Hospital after it attended the fair at about 18:50 BST.Two ambulances and three rapid response vehicles were sent to the scene, the service said.

schema.headline: Children and a woman injured on Maltby fairground ride

title: PlayStation gambles with 18-rated Wolverine game - does it pay off?
description: Image source, Sony/MarvelByTom GerkenTechnology reporterOn Tuesday, Sony will release Marvel's Wolverine - the biggest game exclusive to the PlayStati
body: Image source, Sony/MarvelByTom GerkenTechnology reporterOn Tuesday, Sony will release Marvel's Wolverine - the biggest game exclusive to the PlayStation 5 this year.It's made by Insomniac, the studio responsible for the recent Spider-Man titles, which have sold 50 million copies in recent years.But unlike the friendly neighbourhood superhero, Wolverine has a Pegi-18 rating in the UK, meaning a child cannot legally buy the game, and it contains considerable levels of blood, gore and violence.It represents a gamble for the studio responsible for some of Sony's biggest hits - will it turn out to have been worth it?This review does not reveal the game's biggest moments, but beware minor spoilers for some of the characters that appear and a few early sequences. Some of the images contain blood.Figure caption, Watch: The BBC’s Tom Gerken gets his claws on Marvel's WolverineYou play as Logan, aka Wolverine, the comic book superhero that can self-heal and has retractable claws.Donning the famous yellow-and-black outfit (among others), you hack and slash your way through hordes of enemies. The combat is free-flowing and easy to pick up, as Wolverine stabs and slices his foes with copious amounts of blood on display. Still, some may feel it doesn't go far enough.Image source, Sony/MarvelImage caption, Combat is built around a "rage" meter which fills as you take down enemies, with a full meter turning your surroundings grey and allowing you to swiftly dispatch your foesThere are some stealth options, but I generally ignored them and went in with my claws out. The game didn't penalise me for this.You also unlock a slew of abilities, much like other games in the genre, meaning you get even more powerful as the game rumbles on.And a clever system allows you to spend the rage you have accumulated to regenerate your health.The combat kept me hooked the whole way through the game, which took about 20 hours to get to the end credits. My colleague was faster, clocking in at about 15 hours.Image source, Sony/MarvelImage caption, You briefly mash the square button to regenerate your health after being beaten - meaning so long as you keep up your rage meter, you effectively can't loseWhen Spider-Man released in 2018, it set a new standard for superhero games with an open-world New York City which you could freely (and entertainingly) explore by web-slinging through the skies.It was so influential that it spawned a popular online gag, pointing fun at reviewers who couldn't help but repeat a cliché, external about the game making them feel like Spider-Man."There's a significant shake-up happening here in game design terms," freelance game critic Emma Kent told me."Insomniac is moving away from Spider-Man's open world formula to adopt a linear structure for Wolverine. "That means less open exploration, and a more curated path through the game world." Image source, Sony/MarvelImage caption, The combat is broken up by short sequences where you explore high-detailed environments, which while fun at first began to drag as the game went onIt adds to the gamble that comes with the game having such graphic violence. "Peter Parker and Miles Morales would go out of their way to avoid killing enemies - stringing them up or gluing them against walls with his webs - and there was no real gore to speak of," Kent said. "Some games truly revel in showing detailed and over-exaggerated gore, but the violence in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't feel particularly gratuitous. "When you build up a sense of flow, it really does feel like you're rampaging through dozens of enemies, and I think the blood splashes are an important way of displaying the carnage you're causing." The reality is by having a higher age rating than Spider-Man, it is by definition reducing the amount of people who can buy the game. And the game's director Mike Daly accepted this came with a risk."Even though this character appeals to kids, making a game that is explicitly like, 'sorry, this is not for kids, you should not play this game' - it does reduce the scope," he said."But I think there was no other way to do it. That was the cost of doing business if we really wanted to set a game with this character in this universe."Image source, Sony/MarvelImage caption, The graphics are great, but small cutscenes like this broke up the action too frequently for my tasteOne thing I didn't expect was the game's reliance on its performers. Gameplay is frequently interrupted with cutscenes, which will I'm sure prove divisive.Nonetheless, the acting is top drawer, with the standout being veteran performer Troy Baker (known for many roles including Joel in The Last of Us) who puts in a memorable performance as Nathaniel Essex.Liam McIntyre, who plays Wolverine, told BBC Newsbeat he was "looking forward to people playing it"."I'm so proud that people are resonating with the story, with the performances, the character," he said. "This is such an astoundingly good character piece. "I'm so happy that I've been able to make a Wolverine that hopefully people love."And to that point - when Hugh Jackman's famous take on the character last appeared on the big screen in 2024's Deadpool & Wolverine, it made $205m (then £160m) on opening weekend in the US - the best ever opening for an R-rated film.It all suggests Sony's gamble may be a safer bet than it first seems.Image source, DisneyImage caption, Deadpool & Wolverine ultimately grossed $1.3bn worldwide at the box office,  suggesting there was a much bigger audience than expected for 18-rated violenceThe way you leap from building to building is superb, and feels excellent to control.But I'd rather there had been fewer acting sequences and more gameplay. On one or two occasions, in a cutscene Wolverine did something which felt like it broke a cardinal rule of game design to me - never show the player something cool when you could have let them do it themselves.Still - the performances are of a high quality."Troy and Liam in particular are performers where they get really invested in their characters and subject matter," Daly said."They are part of the problem solving squad for who they are and how they bring that out - they brought a lot to the table."They went above and beyond, and I think that's a big part of what made it so good."Image source, Sony/MarvelImage caption, Criminal Minds actress Nicole Pacent makes an excellent Mystique (right), while Spartacus lead Liam McIntyre is superb as WolverineI'll avoid discussing the story so as not to spoil it, but suffice to say I was engaged, even if at times I felt I was spending too long watching videos and not enough time using the controller.Clearly the developers were inspired by narrative adventures like Uncharted for this kind of storytelling, and the gameplay even feels similar at times with chase and climbing sequences.And while that game was genre-defining, it came out almost 20 years ago, so it's hardly a favourable comparison.In fact, perhaps the biggest issue for Wolverine is that it doesn't reinvent the wheel like Spider-Man did.It's a game packed with tight combat and excellent performances, but it never threatens to meet the genre-defining heights of Insomniac's previous offering.And Daly said there was a "monumental" amount of pressure that came with making the game following the success of Spider-Man - but as to whether the gamble paid off, he took a Zen view."I measure success when I hear people talk to me about the game, who are Wolverine fans, and they say 'thank you for making this, you nailed it'," he said. "If I hear that, it's like, yes, we did it. That's what we set out to do."

schema.headline: PlayStation gambles with 18-rated Wolverine game - does it pay off?

title: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics
description: At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston
body: At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham. The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground. In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL)."I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth. His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normany in France. On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings. "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said."This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.The website for Patriot Platform was registered on 18 May this year, two days after a big anti-immigration "Unite the Kingdom" march in London.Thomas, its most visible founder, first posted about the group on YouTube on 8 June."We need to be a bit smarter," he said, referencing arrests or offences including the assaults on police officers and violent disorder during recent Unite the Kingdom marches, that had been organised by Robinson. "Good men and women are now away from the fight stuck in jail cells." Thomas told his supporters he had a few ideas that would be "more powerful than committing acts of violence and criminal damage".There needs to be a "different MO", he said. "We are looking for the strong, the able, the ones that are willing to do things a bit different."What sets Patriot Platform apart is the scale and co-ordination of their action, says William Allchorn of Anglia Ruskin University, an expert on far-right movements. "There hasn't [previously] been co-ordinated mass activism with hundreds of people descending and trying to take matters, as it were, into their own hands," he says.Thomas spent the summer posting further videos about the group and staging meetings in the North West, Essex, Leicester and Kent. He said he was trying to organise a "mass resistance" movement.What happened in Dover demonstrated some of his new ways of working. The protesters were almost exclusively male. They arrived in well-organised waves in the backs of lorries. They did not engage with the media, and said little to members of the public whose journeys and weekends they were disrupting.Then, after a few hours, before the police could get organised, the men all marched off to Dover Priory Station and left. Estimates vary as to how many were there but it looks like between 200 and 500.The anti-racism group Hope Not Hate said Patriot Platform should be seen "for what it is: a far-right network of men happy to intimidate and inconvenience an entire town for what was effectively a publicity stunt".Nick Lowles, the group's CEO, said Thomas had "been upfront about his intention to create a 'patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom'".At a protest outside the Daily Mail offices in London on Wednesday, Thomas could be seen giving clear instructions to his supporters about his preferred tactics."Don't intimidate anyone," he ordered. "No one talk. Keep a distance. Five metres away from police".Patriot Platform is coming into a crowded space of activists campaigning against immigration. Robinson's is the most high-profile brand. A former close associate of Danny Thomas, Robinson (whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon) has given Patriot Platform public support since Saturday. But there is also Paul Golding's Britain First, Turning Point UK and the neo-Nazi Patriotic Alternative.Thomas was once close to Ryan Bridge, the founder of a group called Raise the Colours, who have put up flags in towns across England over the last year. But the pair have since publicly fallen out, with Thomas telling Bridge in an online rant: "Do I need to stab you in the eye?"Thomas was jailed for two years in 2016 after he and two others tried to kidnap a man at knifepoint in Portsmouth in a dispute over money linked to drugs. What seems to be different about Patriot Platform's approach now is that Thomas is explicitly talking about creating a "voting bloc" of supporters to back a yet-to-be decided party, which offers policies closest to what he wants, at the next general election."I do not support any political party at this moment in time," he said, adding that once the bloc was established, it would be made "extremely clear" which way the group's vote would go. It's not clear whether Reform UK would get his backing. In a public confrontation with Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth on Monday, Thomas complained that Nigel Farage had branded his Dover protest "disgusting"."The working class do not vote," Thomas said. "We are going to make it a fashionable thing to take all your family members to the voting booth."But if your leader keeps slandering people, it's going to push them to other parties."Waiting in the wings is the new party Restore Britain, launched by Rupert Lowe after he was suspended from Reform UK. On X, the party said it "stands with the patriots peacefully protesting against the invasion".  It is not clear how much support Thomas has. Parties like Reform and Restore will be very aware of the potential power that activists like Thomas and Robinson can now wield with their large social media followings. On X, Robinson has two million followers to Farage's 2.3 million, while Thomas has almost 163,000.At Wednesday's protest, Thomas offered to pay supporters for any work they had missed to be there - in cash.This kind of generosity might help explain why his activism - and that of his some-time mentor Robinson - have such a strong Christian message now. The Christian right in America can be a good source of funds.Christianity is now a big part of Danny Thomas's brand. His calls for action are peppered with the occasional "Amen", pronounced in the American way, with the first syllable said "ay" rather than "ah".He was pictured at St Lawrence church in south London in February and March.The local diocese told BBC News that while it welcomed "people of various political and ideological perspectives", it remained "committed to the inclusion of all people" and the focus of worship would "always be the person of Christ, who is for everyone".Thomas has spoken publicly about his new-found faith: "I have repented my sins and, under Jesus Christ, I am a new man."Thomas is trying to raise money for Patriot Platform through a popular American Christian crowdfunding platform. Just below the "Give" and "Share" buttons, there is a "Pray" button.On the page, Thomas says he is trying to raise £5,000 a month to pay for the likes of transport, boats and a studio. This month alone he has raised around £9,000. This attempt to build Christianity into the brand is potentially also a way of painting the UK as a Christian country, and Muslim immigrants as outsiders.As for what comes next for the Patriot Platform after its initial surge in supporters, far-right expert Allchorn thinks it's an unclear picture."A lot of these groups don't really have an end goal in mind," he says. "This often comes kind of later on when they are kind of forced to to come up with more concrete proposals and goals."

schema.headline: Anti-migrant activists like Danny Tommo are changing tactics

title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
description: Figure caption, Watch: MPs share personal stories in assisted dying debateByRichard WheelerPolitical reporterUpdated 1 hour agoMPs have voted against
body:
Figure caption, Watch: MPs share personal stories in assisted dying debateByRichard WheelerPolitical reporterUpdated 1 hour agoMPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term.The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session. Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved.MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.
            Please upgrade your browser to view this interactive
        There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading.Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults have in other countries.The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day."The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Opponents of the assisted dying bill react after MPs voted against itEdwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today. "It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."Labour peer and former Home Secretary Lord Blunkett told the BBC's Newsnight programme that it was a "bad day for democracy".The issue was "clearly not going away" and would re-emerge "in a year or two's time", he added.Figure caption, Watch: A 'bad day for democracy', says Labour peerThose in favour of a change in the law have said they will try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed the MPs' decision.In a joint statement, they said: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law."But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill."They said there was a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying".Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks".She added she still believed law change was "inevitable".Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive".He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect."Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Supporters of assisted dying react in Parliament Square following the vote in the CommonsThe bill in the last parliamentary session, brought forward by Leadbeater, cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments.Edwards brought forward the proposals again in a bid to ensure peers could "finish their job", although this will no longer take place.During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it.She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms".The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother had died alone in October of last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life.Hazelgrove argued "not all pain can be palliated" as she spoke in favour of the bill.Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient".Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon called for a change in the law and described the bill as "better than what we currently have, which offers no safeguards and no protections for people in those final moments".Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not vote on the bill on Friday, previously describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide". He has previously said he personally believes that funding for end-of-life care in the UK should be improved before legalising assisted dying is considered.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? Share your experience

title: 70 Up: Curtain falls on documentary that has captivated Brits for six decades
description: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing outImage source, ITVImage caption, 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter
body: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing outImage source, ITVImage caption, 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter Davies, Symon Basterfield, Paul Kligerman, Tony Walker Neil Hughes, John Brisby, Andrew Brackfield, Bruce Balden Jackie Bassett, Suzy Lusk, Sue DavisByGeorge WrightSix decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister.It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up.The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age."They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood.Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years.Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday.Image source, ITVImage source, ITV"We didn't really know what we were doing, we had no idea what was happening," Jackie said of the day the Granada TV crew turned up at her school.In the first episode, Jackie appeared alongside her friends, Lynn and Sue, as they were asked questions about boys at school and their hopes for the future. Jackie said she would like to marry a boy "that's not got a lot of money, but has got some money".The nation was also introduced to the likes of wide-eyed Neil, who explained his plans to become either an astronaut or a coach driver; anxious Paul, who ruminated on the idea of one day marrying a woman who made him eat his greens; and pensive Bruce, who said his "heart's desire is to see my daddy who is 6,000 miles away" in Rhodesia.Image source, ITVImage caption, In 7 Up, friends Jackie Bassett, Lynn Johnson and Sue Davis were asked questions about boys and their hopes for the futureImage source, ITVImage caption, 7 Up was intended to be a one-off snapshot of the class system in BritainThe first episode was directed by Canadian Paul Almond, with the help of a young researcher named Michael Apted, who was involved in selecting the children.Apted then decided to follow up on the children seven years later."The material was dreadful – as teenagers, they wouldn't say anything," he later said of the second episode, 7 Plus Seven."Yet we started to realise the power of the idea; despite the film not being very good, everyone was interested in it."Apted went on to become a big name in Hollywood, directing blockbusters including James Bond's The World Is Not Enough, but he always returned to the show and said it was his most significant achievement.Every seven years, millions would tune in for updates on the cast's lives. Neil's dreamy outlook on the world as a child descended into battles with depression, isolation and homelessness, only to turn up as a Liberal Democrat councillor at 42 and then a lay preacher seven years later.Jackie initially said she did not want children, but by 42 Up was an adoring mother to three boys.Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Neil Hughes had battles with depression and homelessness but went on to be a Liberal Democrat councillor and a lay preacherAs the series grew in popularity, Apted started receiving push-back from some of the participants, who felt they had been typecast based on their backgrounds.At 21, Apted asked Jackie - who had recently got married - whether she had met "enough men" before she decided to marry. For the rest of the interview, she mostly looked to the floor while Sue and Lynn answered questions.It took her 18 years to fully confront Apted over his questioning.In 49 Up, she told him: "I was really angry… you wouldn't have asked some of the other people in this program that question. You will edit this program as you see fit, I've got no control over that."Recalling the tense exchange, Jackie said she felt Apted could be out of touch, particularly over the changing roles of women in society."I think he still thought we were all in the kitchen, as I mentioned to him at 21. I just thought, 'No, come on, it's about time one of us called you out on it, because he never never asked us questions about politics. It was nearly always domestic," she said.Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Jackie, Lynn and Sue filming 28 Up... Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, ... and filming 35 Up with director Michael Apted on the left Jackie was not the only cast member to clash with Apted.John Brisby, who became a leading barrister, declared in 35 Up that the show felt like a "little pill of poison" injected into his veins every seven years and he wished his headmaster had never put him up for the show. He appeared in later series but refused to be interviewed by Apted.And Charles Furneaux, who later worked at the BBC before becoming commissioning editor at Channel 4, refused to appear after 21 Up following an off-camera argument in which Apted later admitted he went "berserk".Apted acknowledged flaws with the show, saying it was a "horrible error" to have only four women in a cast of 14 when making the original selection.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Michael Apted became a Hollywood director, but always returned to the showFive years ago, Apted passed away, aged 79.The effect he had on the cast is clear in the final episode.Despite their differences, Jackie maintains deep affection and respect for the man she said "opened up a world to me that I would never have known"."I've always said it's a bit like having an uncle in the family. Sometimes you love him and cuddle him to death, and other times you think: I wish he'd just go away."He would always, always help anybody and anything."Nick Hitchon died from cancer in 2023, becoming the second member of the cast to pass away after Lynn Johnson 10 years earlier.Nick, who was born on a farm in the Yorkshire Dales and famously said he wanted to "find out about the moon and all that" in 7 Up, went on to become a scientist and professor at the University of Wisconsin.In his obituary, his brother Andrew wrote Nick "was an expert in nuclear fusion who eventually accepted that he would always be best known for appearing in a ground-breaking TV documentary rather than as a scientist".Image source, ITVImage caption, Nick Hitchon, who went on to become a scientist, passed away in 2023After Apted's death, it was unclear whether 70 Up would happen.But it was announced earlier this year that Asif Kapadia, best known for his documentaries on Amy Winehouse and Diego Maradona, would direct the final chapter.Jackie said she felt apprehensive about having anyone other than Apted in charge, but said Kapadia made her feel immediately at ease. She even welcomed a new approach, saying his interviews felt more like a conversation, while Apted would often leave long, awkward pauses once she had finished her answer.In the final episode, Jackie appears the most content she has been since the age of seven. She attributes this newfound peace to recently moving to Norfolk, from Scotland, where she had been since her thirties. She loves being a mother and grandmother, but said she "needed time for me"."I have that peace around me," she said.Image source, ITVImage caption, Jackie says it is the right time to draw the show to a closeAnd does this episode really mark the end?"I'm not sure any of us will have the energy for it, to be honest," Jackie said. "I think this is the right time to stop, I really do. "Seventy has got a symmetry to it," she said. "We started at seven, we finished at 70 - and that's it."Despite all the plaudits, Jackie has always been slightly perplexed as to why the show has made such an impact, but understands how watching their journeys has helped some people make sense of their own.The series started out being about class but "then they suddenly thought, hang on a minute, this is about life", she said."There's somebody on that programme that just about everybody can associate with. And I think that is something that will outlast all of us."

schema.headline: 70 Up: Curtain falls on documentary that has captivated Brits for six decades

title: The mission to recover Nims Purja's body from Broad Peak
description: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of allFigure caption, Watch: Mingma G recalls the climb to bring
body: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of allFigure caption, Watch: Mingma G recalls the climb to bring home the bodies of his friendsByCarrie DaviesPakistan correspondentReporting fromIslamabadAs he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him."I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."Image source, Mingma GImage caption, Mingma G embarked on a difficult journey after learning his good friends had diedMingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following. In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.Image source, AFPImage caption, Nirmal Purja was an accomplished mountaineer who put Nepalese climbers on the map Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant." But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened."That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."Image source, Mingma GImage caption, Mingma G's old friend Kilu was among those who climbed Broad Peak with NimsOn 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Trekkers saw these climbers from Nims's group near the summit of Broad PeakThe group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak"."We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.Figure caption, Watch: Moment deadly avalanche crashes down Broad PeakBy the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.But something was bothering him.One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors."I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.Image caption, Purja's coordinates according to Garmin's data. Mingma G says they did not find Nims's Garmin watch on his bodyHe wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once."Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.Image source, Sirbaz KhanImage caption, The recovery operation was carried out on foot because helicopters were not immediately availableOn 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, As news spread of the disaster, there were vigils in Nepal paying tribute to the climbers The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall."They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families. Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The bodies of Nims, Kilu and Gyaljen Sherpa arrived in Kathmandu on 11 August Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

schema.headline: The mission to recover Nims Purja's body from Broad Peak

title: Ben Delo: Reform receives record £36m donation from cryptocurrency billionaire
description: Reform UK has received a £36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.Writing in the Daily Telegraph, e
body: Reform UK has received a £36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.Writing in the Daily Telegraph, external, Ben Delo said he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK.Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.Delo said he was donating £1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future. There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.But Labour previously introduced a £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated £4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong in order to continue his backing for the party.Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.In the Telegraph, Delo wrote: "Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of 'our democracy' while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field."My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."Reform's fundraising has been under scrutiny with police announcing an investigation over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.The party denied any wrongdoing and said it would co-operate with the investigation.Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m cash gift he received from Thailand-based cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne ahead of the 2024 election upon his election as an MP.Farage argues he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.The Metropolitan Police is also investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.The police inquiry is looking at donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell.It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.The restrictions on donations from Britons living abroad prompted a furious row with Reform and its key donors, who have accused Labour of trying to stymie their party's progress.The government has also sought to prevent overseas voters moving to the UK from giving more than £100,000 for a year after their arrival as part of the Representation of the People Bill, which has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.Last year Harborne gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - which was the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person at the time.The Conservatives had received £10m as a legacy but that too has been eclipsed by Delo's latest donation.Responding to the donation, a Labour Party spokesperson said Farage was "still up to his neck in scandal" and "the questions he faces aren't going away - in fact they're piling up"."Reform UK can't buy their way out of questions about sleaze, criminal mates and dodgy finances," they said. "It's time Farage and Reform finally came clean with the public, co-operated fully with the police, and proved they're not just in it for themselves."Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson Lisa Smart said Farage wanted to "bring Trump's America to our shores by buying his way into power". "He's trying to get into Number 10 as if it's a stop on a monopoly board," the Liberal Democrat added. "It can't go on like this. Andy Burnham needs to introduce a cap on political donations. Our democracy depends on it."

title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after attending brother King Harald's funeral
description: Princess Astrid of Norway, the sister of the late King Harald V, has died at the age of 94, two days after attending his funeral, the country's royal
body: Princess Astrid of Norway, the sister of the late King Harald V, has died at the age of 94, two days after attending his funeral, the country's royal palace has announced.The new king, Haakon VIII, said that "throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner".Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years as king. His funeral was Astrid's last public engagement.The princess will be buried at state expense and flags will be flown at half-mast across Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.Astrid was the last surviving child of King Olav V, who reigned from 1957 to 1991.She became Norway's first lady at the age of 22 in 1954, after the death of her mother Crown Princess Märtha. Olav did not remarry and Astrid retained the title until her brother's marriage in 1968."In her work, Princess Astrid was always particularly concerned with care and inclusion for the most vulnerable in society," her nephew King Haakon said in his statement.Her health had deteriorated in recent months and in March she received hospital treatment for pneumonia.Dozens of European royals and heads of state attended Harald's funeral on Wednesday, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings.Thousands of people lined the route during a procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon.The non-royal leaders paying their respects included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and five foreign prime ministers.

schema.headline: Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after attending brother King Harald's funeral
